name: Tara Usman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thanks for talking with me. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start: tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Mostly it's a bus and a lot of waiting. I'm doing nursing, so Monday and Tuesday are lectures on anatomy and a skills lab where we practise making a bed with a patient in it, which is harder than it sounds. Wednesday I'm at the supermarket checkout from five till ten, and I work all day Saturday too. I live with my mum and my little brother, so I do my reading at the kitchen table after he's asleep.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's the part of this first term that worries you most?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Money, honestly. The loan pays my fees and that's it. I've got maybe twenty pounds spare at the end of a month, and my mum can't help because she's already stretched on rent. I got in with average grades, so there's no scholarship cushion. If my checkout hours drop one week, I feel it straight away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: I'll read you a short picture called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, because it means the world carries on like it is. Nurses are still needed, and people still need to eat so the shop still needs staff. At the supermarket we've got self-checkouts already and nobody's lost their job over them yet. I wouldn't make a fuss about it with friends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd still be worried, just about different things. Rent for my mum, my loan, and whether I pass the placement exam in the spring. AI doing a bit of paperwork isn't what keeps me up. Being broke while I'm still training is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on exactly as now. Keep the Saturday shifts, keep the two evenings, and try to pick up one more evening if the manager offers. I'd put five pounds a week in a jar for my uniform and placement travel. I wouldn't change course or try anything new.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Flat, a bit tired. Not scared of the technology, but scared of the bills. It's a quiet kind of stress, the sort where you check your bank app twice before buying lunch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said hours at the checkout matter a lot. What happens in a month when they drop?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: When hours drop, I skip the bus and walk forty minutes each way to save the fare. Last winter my mum and I had cereal for tea twice in one week. I'd rather do that than borrow from anyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you use any AI tools yourself, for study or anything else?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, never. I don't trust it and nobody's shown me why I need it. My lecturer said some students use it for essays, and I'd rather be slow and do it myself. If it's mostly hype, I've lost nothing by ignoring it.

say: I'd tell friends it's **mostly hype** and the world carries on as normal.
At work I'd say the self-checkouts **haven't cost jobs** so far.
think: Privately my worry is **money**, not AI: my mum's rent, my loan and my placement costs.
I'd still be **anxious** about hours dropping, because I live on under a month of savings.
do: Keep the Saturday and two evening **checkout shifts** and ask for a third if one comes up.
Put **five pounds a week** in a jar for uniform and placement travel.
Walk to campus instead of taking the bus when the week is tight.
feel: Tired and **flat**, a quiet money stress more than fear of technology.
S0.quote: Not scared of the technology, but scared of the bills. It's a quiet kind of stress, the sort where you check your bank app twice before buying lunch.
fieldNote: Tara's worry is her own **thin cushion**, not AI; she brushed past the technology within seconds.
Strong **resistance** to AI: she has never used it and sees no reason to start.
Mood is anxious even in the calm scenario, because one lost shift hits her budget.

steps.text: Keep the Saturday and two evening checkout shifts
Save five pounds a week in a jar for placement travel
Walk forty minutes to campus when money is tight

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: I'll read you a short picture called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's worrying for office people, but we'll always need nurses. You can't have a computer turn someone over in bed or hold a hand. But I'd say the government should step in with training money, because people are going to be pushed around.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm not sure nursing is fully safe. A lot of what nurses write up, like notes and checking doses, software could take. And my checkout job is the sort of work that goes first. So I could lose my wage and still be years from a nursing salary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my head down, pass my modules and try to get a hospital healthcare-assistant job on the ward bank for weekends, because that is closer to nursing than the till. I'd ask my union rep at the shop what happens if they cut checkouts. I still wouldn't touch AI tools, I'd learn from the nurses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy and a bit angry. Angry that companies get the gains and we get told to adapt. I voted for people who promised support, and I'd want them to follow through.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which tasks at the supermarket do you think software would take first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The scanning, the bagging help, the stock ordering. Our manager already uses a tablet to count shelves. I think the checkout team shrinks from twelve people to maybe five, and I'm the newest, so I'd go first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your mum about your degree choice if nursing jobs started shrinking?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say stay on the course, because care work is about people. But I'd also tell my mum honestly that I'm nervous, since she's never hidden bills from me. I'd rather say it straight than pretend.

say: I'd say **nurses stay needed**, but government must fund retraining for everyone pushed out.
I'd tell my mum I'm staying on the course but I'm **nervous**.
think: I fear my **checkout wage** goes first, years before any nursing salary arrives.
Some nursing paperwork and dose checks could move to software, so I'm **not fully sure** it's safe.
do: Apply for a **healthcare-assistant** weekend job on the hospital staff bank.
Ask my **union rep** at the supermarket what happens if checkouts are cut.
Keep passing modules and learn from the ward nurses rather than AI tools.
feel: **Uneasy**, with some anger that companies keep the gains and ordinary people are told to adapt.
S1.quote: Companies get the gains and we get told to adapt. I voted for people who promised support, and I'd want them to follow through.
fieldNote: Her **progressive** views come through: union, public training money and anger at employers.
She sees nursing as safer than checkout work but not fully safe, a **sensible split**.
Newest on the checkout team, so she expects to be first cut.

steps.text: Apply for a weekend healthcare-assistant job on the hospital staff bank
Ask the union rep what happens if checkouts are cut
Vote for parties that promise retraining money

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: I'll read you a short picture called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a disaster for ordinary people, and nobody asked us. Two years is nothing. My mum's not going to understand it, my brother's eleven, and there's no plan from anyone. I'd be posting that the government has to freeze rents and bills while this gets sorted.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd be frightened. I'd have just finished one year of nursing, and my shop job would be gone fast. The hands-on nursing part gets a few more years, but I wouldn't have the money to reach the end of the degree. And nobody can tell me if hospitals would still hire students.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably try to hold on to the checkout job as long as I could, take every extra shift, and keep the savings jar going. I'd ask the course tutor straight out what happens to placements. I'd go to the council office and ask about help for people on loans. I wouldn't know what else to do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Everything I planned depended on a three-year degree and a job at the end. I can't plan past next month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With only two years, what changes about your degree plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd pause nothing yet. I'd finish the year, because if care work stays human for those extra three years then it's the safest thing I've got. But I'd have no wage to pay for it, so I'd end up leaning on a loan I might never repay on a nurse's pay that might not exist.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you lean on, if anyone, if your wage disappeared?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mum, but she can't do much. Maybe the neighbours, we know a few families on our road who help each other with food and lifts. Mostly I'd lean on a government that I'd want to step up, because nobody else can cover this.

say: I'd say **two years is nothing** and ordinary people need rent and bill protection now.
I'd tell the tutor to give a straight answer on **placements**.
think: I'm **frightened**: the checkout job vanishes first and I can't afford to finish the degree.
Nursing might stay human a few extra years, but I'd be **borrowing** for a job that may not exist.
do: Take **every extra shift** at the supermarket while it lasts.
Visit the **council office** to ask about help for students on loans.
Finish the year and ask my tutor what happens to **placements**.
feel: **Alarmed**, unable to plan past next month because the whole three-year plan collapses.
S2.quote: Everything I planned depended on a three-year degree and a job at the end. I can't plan past next month.
fieldNote: The short warning hits Tara hardest because she has **no cushion** and her mum cannot help.
She looks to **government and neighbours**, not to AI tools or personal reinvention.
Alarmed rather than panicked because she still has a plan: finish the year and ask questions.

steps.text: Take every extra checkout shift while the job lasts
Ask the council office about help for students on loans
Finish the first year and ask my tutor about placements

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: I'll read you a short picture called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's serious but it gives us a chance. Five years is long enough to finish my degree and work a bit. I'd say governments need to start now on training, rent help and a safety net, not wait for 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd still feel behind. I'd qualify in about three years, so I'd have two years as a nurse before the thinking AI is everywhere, and then the robots come later. That's actually a window where nursing may be one of the last jobs standing. I'm cautiously okay with that, but I'd worry about my mum.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish nursing, work on the ward bank at weekends, and save the extra money properly in a savings account, not a jar. I'd also ask my mum to look at cheaper housing. I'd join the student nurses' union branch, because a group of us is louder than one person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit calmer than the last one. Still a weight, but there's a route through. It feels like climbing a hill rather than falling off a cliff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do five years give you that two don't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years means I could qualify and have an income and a registration number. Two years means I'd be stuck in the middle with debt and no certificate. That difference is huge for someone like me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still do nursing if you knew this was coming?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, I would. It's the one thing I was sure of when I picked it. People will still be ill and scared, and someone has to sit with them at three in the morning. Whatever AI does with the charts, that part stays ours for a while.

say: I'd say **five years is enough** to finish a degree, but governments must start training and rent help now.
I'd join the **student nurses' union branch** and say groups are louder than one person.
think: Nursing could be among the **last jobs standing** because the hands-on robots come later.
I still worry about my **mum's rent** while I'm paying my way through.
do: Finish the degree and work the **ward bank** at weekends.
Move savings into a proper **savings account** instead of a jar.
Join the student nurses' **union branch** this term.
feel: A bit **calmer**: it feels like climbing a hill rather than falling off a cliff.
S3.quote: Five years means I could qualify and have an income and a registration number. Two years means I'd be stuck in the middle with debt and no certificate.
fieldNote: Tara compares **qualifying in time** against being stranded with debt, which explains the lower mood.
Her **collective** instinct stays strong: union branch, group voice, public safety net.
She still carries her mum's rent worry, so uneasy rather than calm.

steps.text: Finish the nursing degree and work the ward bank at weekends
Move savings from a jar into a proper savings account
Join the student nurses' union branch this term

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: I'll read you a short picture called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's fair warning and we should use it. Ten years is a whole career's first stretch. I'd say schools should start teaching how to work with machines, and governments should start building the safety net right away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, ten years is comfortable. I'd qualify, pay down a chunk of my loan, maybe do a specialist course in something like children's or elderly care. The thinking AI will be there in 2036, but hands-on care stays human until about 2039. I'd feel fine, if my mum's okay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work hard at the degree, then take a staff nurse job and start saving a tenth of my pay. I'd consider a specialism like district nursing. I might even try an AI tool at some point, once someone I trust shows me. I'd also help my brother choose a trade that suits him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly steady. A little excited actually, like I've got time to build something. The only dark patch is my mum getting older with no safety net.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With ten years, what would you do differently from now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop cutting every corner. At the moment I live shift to shift. In ten years I'd have a salary, a home I can rent in my own name, and maybe a little in savings. That is real peace for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your brother, who's eleven?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him to learn something with his hands and his head, and not to follow money alone. I'd say to be kind and curious, because those are the skills machines are worst at. And I'd tell him I'll help.

say: I'd say ten years is **fair warning** and schools should teach working alongside machines.
I'd tell my brother to learn a skill with his **hands and his head**.
think: Ten years is **comfortable**: I'd qualify, pay down loan and maybe specialise in elderly care.
The only dark patch is my **mum getting older** with no safety net.
do: Qualify and take a **staff nurse** job, saving a tenth of every pay.
Consider a **specialist course** such as district nursing.
Try one **AI tool** if someone I trust shows me how.
feel: Mostly **steady** and a little excited, like there's time to build something.
S4.quote: At the moment I live shift to shift. In ten years I'd have a salary, a home I can rent in my own name, and maybe a little in savings.
fieldNote: Even with ten years, Tara's **money fear** from her thin cushion keeps her at uneasy rather than calm.
Only here does she soften on **AI tools**, and only if a trusted person shows her.
She turns to **family-minded** plans: helping her brother, caring for her mum.

steps.text: Save a tenth of every staff nurse pay
Take a specialist course such as district nursing
Try one AI tool once a trusted nurse shows me
Help my brother choose a trade that suits him

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, the quick one. I'd have the least time and the least money, and a whole degree half done. What would help is a government that pays for student nurses properly, caps rents, and tells us early what hospitals will still hire for. And a tutor who's honest.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: No, I think you got most of it. Just that people like me aren't scared of the new things, we're scared of paying for them. I'd like someone in charge to say that out loud.

headlineQuote: People like me aren't scared of the new things, we're scared of paying for them.
portrait: Tara is **19**, a first-year nursing student living with her mum and little brother, working checkout shifts on a **thin cushion**.
She is progressive, pro-union and wants **government support** and retraining money rather than personal reinvention.
She resists new technology and has **never used AI**, preferring to learn from nurses on the ward.
Her mood follows money: anxious in mild worlds, **alarmed** at two years and steadier with five or ten.
She believes **hands-on care** stays human longest, which is why nursing still feels like her best bet.
biggestWorry: The **AGI by 2028** picture worries her most: two years, no savings and a half-finished degree.
whatWouldHelp: Proper **government pay** for student nurses, rent caps and early, honest word from tutors on what hospitals will hire.
